entries.9eebae35425ba64f7c1b90a939ef212c13cb6664: <div sID="gen20843" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Zech.6" sID="Zech.6"/> <div eID="gen20843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20844" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20845" type="x-p"/> The two kingdoms of providence and grace are what we are all very nearly interested in, and therefore are concerned to acquaint ourselves with, all our temporal affairs being in a necessary subjection to divine Providence, and all our spiritual and eternal concerns in a necessary dependence upon divine grace; and these two are represented to us in this chapter—the former by a vision, the latter by a type. Here is, I. God, as King of nations, ruling the world by the ministry of angels, in the vision of the four chariots, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.1-Zech.6.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. God, as King of saints, ruling the church by the mediation of Christ, in the figure of Joshua the high priest crowned, the ceremony performed, and then explained concerning Christ, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.9-Zech.6.15">ver. 9-15</reference>.
entries.5a8b829bd0eaa2bff64647b8768b8929f320d214: <div eID="gen20845" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20844" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Four Chariots. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20846" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And I turned, and lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and, behold, there came four chariots out from between two mountains; and the mountains <hi type="italic">were</hi> mountains of brass. <hi type="super">2</hi> In the first chariot <hi type="italic">were</hi> red horses; and in the second chariot black horses; <hi type="super">3</hi> And in the third chariot white horses; and in the fourth chariot grisled and bay horses. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then I answered and said unto the angel that talked with me, What <hi type="italic">are</hi> these, my lord? <hi type="super">5</hi> And the angel answered and said unto me, These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the four spirits of the heavens, which go forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth. <hi type="super">6</hi> The black horses which <hi type="italic">are</hi> therein go forth into the north country; and the white go forth after them; and the grisled go forth toward the south country. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the bay went forth, and sought to go that they might walk to and fro through the earth: and he said, Get you hence, walk to and fro through the earth. So they walked to and fro through the earth. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then cried he upon me, and spake unto me, saying, Behold, these that go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country. <div eID="gen20846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20847" type="x-p"/> The prophet is forward to receive this vision, and, as if he expected it, he <hi type="italic">turned and lifted up his eyes and looked.</hi> Though this was the seventh vision he had had, yet he did not think he had had enough; for the more we know of God and his will, if we know it aright, the more desirous we shall be to get a further acquaintance with God. Now observe here the sight that the prophet had of<hi type="italic">four chariots</hi> drawn by horses of divers colours, together with the explication of the sight, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.1-Zech.6.5">v. 1-5</reference>. He did not look long before he discovered that which was worth seeing, and which would serve very much for the encouraging of himself and his friends in this dark day. We are very much in the dark concerning the meaning of this vision. Some by the <hi type="italic">four chariots</hi> understand the four monarchies; and then they read (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">These are the four winds of the heavens,</hi> and suppose that therein reference is had to <reference osisRef="Dan.7.2">Dan. vii. 2</reference>, where Daniel saw, in vision, the <hi type="italic">four winds of the heavens striving upon the great sea,</hi> representing the four monarchies. The Babylonian monarchy, they think, is here represented by the <hi type="italic">red horses,</hi> which are not afterwards mentioned, because that monarchy was now extinct. The second chariot with the <hi type="italic">black horses</hi> is the Persian monarchy, which went forth northward against the Babylonians, and <hi type="italic">quieted God's Spirit in the north country,</hi> by executing his judgments on Babylon and freeing the Jews from their captivity. The <hi type="italic">white,</hi> the Grecians, go <hi type="italic">forth after them</hi> in the north, for they overthrow the Persians. The <hi type="italic">grizzled,</hi> the Romans, who conquered the Grecian empire, are said to <hi type="italic">go forth towards the south country,</hi> because Egypt, which lay southward, was the last branch of the Grecian empire that was subdued by the Romans. The <hi type="italic">bay horses</hi> had been with the <hi type="italic">grizzled,</hi> but afterwards went forth by themselves; and by these they understand the Goths and Vandals, who with their victorious arms walked to and fro through the earth, or the Seleucidæ and Lagidæ, the two branches of the Grecian empire. Thus Grotius and others. <div eID="gen20847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20848" type="x-p"/> But I incline rather to understand this vision more generally, as designing to represent the administration of the kingdom of Providence in the government of this lower world. The <hi type="italic">angels</hi> are often called the <hi type="italic">chariots of God,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Ps. lxviii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10">xviii. 10</reference>. The various providences of God concerning nations and churches are represented by the different colours of horses, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Rev. vi. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.4">4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.5">5,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.8">8</reference>. And so we may observe here, 1. That the counsels and decrees of God are the spring and original of all events, and they are immovable, as <hi type="italic">mountains of brass.</hi> The <hi type="italic">chariots</hi> came <hi type="italic">from between the two mountains;</hi> for God <hi type="italic">performs the thing that is appointed for us:</hi> his appointments are the originals, and his performances are but copies from them; he does all <hi type="italic">according to the counsel of his will.</hi> We could as soon grasp the mountains in our arms as comprehend the divine counsels in our finite understandings, and as soon remove <hi type="italic">mountains of brass</hi> as alter any of God's purposes; for <hi type="italic">he is in one mind, and who can turn him?</hi> Whatever the providences of God are concerning us, as to public or private affairs, we should see them all coming from <hi type="italic">between the mountains of brass,</hi> and therefore see it as much our folly to quarrel with them as it is our duty to acquiesce in them. Who may say to God, <hi type="italic">What doest thou, or why doest thou so?</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.28">iv. 28</reference>. 2. That God executes his decrees in the works of Providence, which are as chariots, in which he rides as a prince in an open chariot, to show his glory to the world, in which, as in chariots of war, he rides forth <hi type="italic">conquering and to conquer,</hi> and triumphing over all the enemies of his glory and government. God is great and terrible in his doings (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.3">Ps. lxvi. 3</reference>), and in them we <hi type="italic">see the goings of our God, our King,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.24">Ps. lxviii. 24</reference>. His providences move swiftly and strongly as chariots, but all directed and governed by his infinite wisdom and sovereign will, as chariots by their drivers. 3. That the holy angels are the ministers of God's providence, and are employed by him, as <hi type="italic">the armies of heaven,</hi> for the executing of his counsels among <hi type="italic">the inhabitants of the earth;</hi> they are the <hi type="italic">chariots,</hi> or, which comes all to one, they are the horses that draw the chariots, great in power and might, and who, like the horse that God himself describes (<reference osisRef="Job.39.19">Job xxxix. 19</reference>, &c.), are clothed with thunder, are terrible, but cannot be <hi type="italic">terrified</hi> nor <hi type="italic">made afraid;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">chariots of fire, and horses of fire,</hi> to carry one prophet to heaven and guard another on earth. They are as observant of and obsequious to the will of God as well-managed horses are to their rider or driver. Not that God needs them or their services, but he is pleased to make use of them, that he may put honour upon them, and encourage our trust in his providence. 4. That the events of Providence have different aspects and the face of the times often changes. The <hi type="italic">horses</hi> in the <hi type="italic">first chariot</hi> were <hi type="italic">red,</hi> signifying war and bloodshed, <hi type="italic">blood to the horse-bridles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.20">Rev. xiv. 20</reference>. Those in the <hi type="italic">second chariot</hi> were <hi type="italic">black,</hi> signifying the dismal melancholy consequences of war; it puts all into mourning, lays all waste, introduces famines, and pestilences, and desolations, and makes whole lands to languish. Those in the <hi type="italic">third chariot</hi> were <hi type="italic">white,</hi> signifying the return of comfort, and peace, and prosperity, after these dark and dismal times: though God cause grief to the children of men, yet will he have compassion. Those in the <hi type="italic">fourth chariot</hi> were of a mixed colour, <hi type="italic">grizzled</hi> and <hi type="italic">bay;</hi> some <hi type="italic">speckled</hi> and <hi type="italic">spotted,</hi> and <hi type="italic">ash-coloured,</hi> signifying events of different complexions interwoven and counter-changed, a day of prosperity and a day of adversity set <hi type="italic">the one over-against the other.</hi> The cup of Providence in the hand of the Lord is<hi type="italic">full of mixture,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.75.8">Ps. lxxv. 8</reference>. 5. That all the instruments of Providence, and all the events of it, come from God, and from him they receive their commissions and instructions (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">These are the four spirits of heaven, the four winds</hi> (so some), which seem to blow as they list, from the various points of the compass; but God has them <hi type="italic">in his fists</hi> and brings them out of <hi type="italic">his treasuries.</hi> Or, rather, These are <hi type="italic">the angels</hi> that <hi type="italic">go forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth,</hi> to attend upon him and minister to him, to behold his glory in the upper world, which is their blessedness, and to serve his glory in their blessedness, and to serve his glory in this lower world, which is their business. They <hi type="italic">stand before him</hi> as the <hi type="italic">Lord of the whole earth,</hi> to receive orders from him and give up their accounts to him concerning their services on this earth, for it is all within his jurisdiction. But, when he appoints, they <hi type="italic">go forth</hi> as messengers of his counsels and ministers of his justice and mercy. Those secret motions and impulses upon the spirits of men by which the designs of Providence are carried on, some think, are these <hi type="italic">four spirits of the heavens,</hi> which <hi type="italic">go forth from God</hi> and fulfil what he appoints, who is <hi type="italic">the God of the spirits of all flesh.</hi> 6. That there is an admirable beauty in Providence, and one event serves for a balance to another (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The black horses went forth,</hi> carrying with them very dark and melancholy events, such as made every person and every thing look black; but presently <hi type="italic">the white went forth after them,</hi> carrying joy to those that mourned, and, by a new turn given to affairs, making them to look pleasant again. Such are God's dealings with his church and people: if the black horses go forth, the white ones presently go after them; for <hi type="italic">as affliction abounds consolation much more abounds.</hi> 7. That the common general aspect of providence is mixed and compounded. The <hi type="italic">grizzled</hi> and <hi type="italic">bay horses</hi> were both in the <hi type="italic">fourth chariot</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.3">v. 3</reference>), and though they went forth, at first, towards the <hi type="italic">south country,</hi> yet afterwards they <hi type="italic">sought to walk to and fro through the earth</hi> and were directed to do so, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.7">v. 7</reference>. If we go to and fro through the earth, we shall find the events of Providence neither all black nor all white, but ash-coloured, or gray, mixed of black and white. Such is the world we live in; that before us is unmixed. Here we are singing, at the same time, of <hi type="italic">mercy and judgment,</hi> and we must <hi type="italic">sing unto God</hi> of both (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.1">Ps. ci. 1</reference>) and labour to accommodate ourselves to God's will and design in the mixtures of Providence, rejoicing in our comforts as though we rejoiced not, because they have their allays, and weeping for our afflictions as though we wept not, because there is so much mercy mixed with them. 8. That God is well-pleased with all the operations of his own providence (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">These have quieted my spirit,</hi> these <hi type="italic">black horses</hi> which denote extraordinary judgments, and the <hi type="italic">white</hi> ones which denote extraordinary deliverances, both which <hi type="italic">went towards the north country,</hi> while the common mixed providences went all the world over. These have <hi type="italic">quieted my spirit in the north-country,</hi> which had of late been the most remarkable scene of action with reference to the church; that is, by these uncommon appearances and actings of providence God's wrath is executed upon the enemies of the church, and his favours are conferred upon the church, both which had long been deferred, and in both God had fulfilled his will, accomplished his word, and so <hi type="italic">quieted his Spirit. The Lord is well-pleased for his righteousness' sake;</hi> and, as he speaks, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Isa. i. 24</reference>, made himself easy.
entries.305684380e3f054d114db43d0d8fc1e7aea9f738: <div eID="gen20848" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Coronation of Joshua; Prediction of the Messiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20849" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">10</hi> Take of <hi type="italic">them of</hi> the captivity, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of Heldai, of Tobijah, and of Jedaiah, which are come from Babylon, and come thou the same day, and go into the house of Josiah the son of Zephaniah; <hi type="super">11</hi> Then take silver and gold, and make crowns, and set <hi type="italic">them</hi> upon the head of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest; <hi type="super">12</hi> And speak unto him, saying, Thus speaketh the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, saying, Behold the man whose name <hi type="italic">is</hi> The BRANCH; and he shall grow up out of his place, and he shall build the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">13</hi> Even he shall build the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the crowns shall be to Helem, and to Tobijah, and to Jedaiah, and to Hen the son of Zephaniah, for a memorial in the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> And they <hi type="italic">that are</hi> far off shall come and build in the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and ye shall know that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath sent me unto you. And <hi type="italic">this</hi> shall come to pass, if ye will diligently obey the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <div eID="gen20849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20850" type="x-p"/> God did not only at <hi type="italic">sundry times,</hi> but <hi type="italic">in divers manners,</hi> speak in time past by the prophets to his church. In the former part of this chapter he spoke by a vision, which only the prophet himself saw; here, in this latter part, he speaks by a sign, or type, which many saw, and which, as it was explained, was an illustrious prediction of the Messiah as the priest and king of his church. Here is, <div eID="gen20850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20851" type="x-p"/> I. The significant ceremony which God appointed, and that was the <hi type="italic">coronation of Joshua</hi> the high priest, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.10-Zech.6.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. It is observable that there should be two eminent types of Christ in the Old Testament that were both named <hi type="italic">Joshua</hi> (the same name with <hi type="italic">Jesus,</hi> and by the LXX., and in the New Testament, rendered <hi type="italic">Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.7.45">Acts vii. 45</reference>)—Joshua the chief captain, a type of Christ the captain of our salvation, and Joshua the chief priest, a type of Christ the high priest of our profession, and both in their day saviours and leaders into Canaan. And this is peculiar to Joshua the high priest, that here was something done to him by the divine appointment on purpose that he might be a type of Christ, a priest after the order of Melchizedek, who was both a king and a priest. Joshua was far from being ambitious of a crown, and the people of having a crowned head over them; but the prophet, to the great surprise of both, is ordered to crown Joshua as if he had been a king. And, as Zerubbabel's prudence and piety kept this from being any affront to him (as the setting up of a rival with him), so God's providence kept the kings of Persia from taking umbrage at it, as raising a rebellion against them. In doing what we are sure is God's pleasure, as this was, we may well venture men's displeasure. 1. Here were some Jews come from Babylon that brought an offering to the house of God, <hi type="italic">some of the captivity,</hi> here named to their honour, that <hi type="italic">came from Babylon</hi> on a visit to Jerusalem. They ought to have bidden a final farewell to Babylon, and to have come and settled with their brethren in their own land, and for their remissness and indifference in not doing so they thought to atone by this visit. Perhaps they came as ambassadors from the body of the Jews that were in Babylon, who lived there in ease and fulness; and, hearing that the building of the temple went on slowly for want of money, they sent them with an offering of gold and silver for the service of the house of God. Note, Those that by reason of distance, or otherwise, cannot forward a good work by their persons, must, as they are able, forward it by their purses; if some find hands, let others fill them. 2. Time and place are appointed for the prophet to meet them. They thought to bring their present to the priest, God's ordinary minister; but God has a prophet, an extraordinary one, ready to receive them and it, which would be an encouragement to them, who, in their captivity, had so often complained, <hi type="italic">We see not our signs, there is no more any prophet,</hi> and would invite them and others to re-settle in their own land, which then began to look like itself, like a holy land, when the Spirit of prophecy was revived in it. Zechariah was ordered to give them the meeting <hi type="italic">the same day</hi> they came (for when they had arrived they would <hi type="italic">lose no time,</hi> but present their offering immediately), and to bid them welcome, assuring them that God now accepted their gifts. He was to meet them in the house of Josiah, the son of Zephaniah, who probably was receiver-general for the temple, and kept the treasures of it. They brought their gold and silver, to be employed about the temple, but God ordered it to be used in honour of One <hi type="italic">greater than the temple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.12.6">Matt. xii. 6</reference>. 3. Crowns are to be <hi type="italic">made,</hi> and <hi type="italic">put upon the head of Joshua,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.6.11">v. 11</reference>. It is supposed that there were two crowns provided, one of silver and the other of gold; the former (as some think) denoting his priestly dignity, the latter his kingly dignity. Or, rather, he being a priest already, and having a crown of gold, of pure gold, already, to signify his honour and power as a priest, these crowns of silver and gold both signify the <hi type="italic">royal dignity,</hi> the crown of silver being perhaps designed to typify the kingdom of the Messiah when he was here on earth, for then he was the <hi type="italic">King of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.49">John i. 49</reference>), but the crown of gold his kingdom in his exalted state, the glory of which as far exceeded that of the former as gold does silver. The sun shines as gold, when he <hi type="italic">goes forth in his strength;</hi> and the beams of the moon, when she <hi type="italic">walks in brightness,</hi> we call <hi type="italic">silver beams.</hi> Those that had worshipped the sun and moon shall now fall down before the golden and silver crowns of the exalted Redeemer, before whom the sun shall be ashamed and the moon confounded, being both out-shone. <div eID="gen20851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20852" type="x-p"/> II. The signification which God gave of this ceremony. Every one would be ready to ask, "What is the meaning of Joshua's being crowned thus?" And the prophet is as ready to tell them the meaning of it. Upon this speaking sign is grafted a prediction, and the sign was used to make it the more taken notice of and the better remembered. Now the promise is, <div eID="gen20852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20853" type="x-p"/> 1. That God will, in the fulness of time, raise up a great high priest, like Joshua. Tell Joshua that he is but the figure of one that is to come, a faint shadow of him (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Speak unto him</hi> in the name of <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> that <hi type="italic">the man whose name is The BRANCH</hi> shall <hi type="italic">grow up out of his place,</hi> out of Bethlehem the city of David, the place appointed for his birth; though the family be a root in a dry ground, yet this branch shall spring out of it, as in the spring, when the sun returns, the flowers spring out of the roots, in which they lay buried out of sight and out of mind. He shall <hi type="italic">grow up for himself</hi> (so some read it) <hi type="italic">propria virtute—by his own vital energy,</hi> shall be exalted <hi type="italic">in his own strength.</hi> <div eID="gen20853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20854" type="x-p"/> 2. That, as Joshua was an active useful instrument in building the temple, so <hi type="italic">the man, the branch,</hi> shall be the master-builder, the sole builder of the spiritual temple, the gospel-church. He <hi type="italic">shall build the temple of the Lord;</hi> and it is repeated (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">Even he shall build the temple of the Lord.</hi> He shall grow up to do good, to be an instrument of God's glory and a great blessing to mankind. Note, The gospel-church is the <hi type="italic">temple of the Lord,</hi> a <hi type="italic">spiritual house</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1 Pet. ii. 5</reference>), a <hi type="italic">holy temple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.21">Eph. ii. 21</reference>. In the temple God made discoveries of himself to his people, and there he received the service and homage of his people; so, in the gospel-church, the light of divine revelation shines by the word, and the spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise are offered. Now Christ is not only the foundation, but the founder, of this temple, by his Spirit and grace. <div eID="gen20854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20855" type="x-p"/> 3. That Christ shall bear the glory. Glory is a burden, but not too heavy for him to bear who upholds all things. The cross was his glory, and he bore that; so was the crown <hi type="italic">an exceeding weight of glory,</hi> and he bears that. The <hi type="italic">government</hi> is <hi type="italic">upon his shoulders,</hi> and in it <hi type="italic">he bears the glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa. ix. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">They shall hang upon him all the glory of his Father's house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.24">Isa. xxii. 24</reference>. It becomes him, and he is <hi type="italic">par negotio—well able to bear it.</hi> The glory of the priesthood and royalty had been divided between the house of Aaron and that of David; but now he alone shall bear all the glory of both. That which he shall bear, which he shall undertake, shall be indeed the <hi type="italic">glory of Israel;</hi> and they must wait for that, and, in prospect of it, must be content in the want of that external glory which they formerly had. He shall bear such a glory as shall make the glory of this latter house greater than that of the former. He shall <hi type="italic">lift up the glory</hi> (so it may be read); the glory of Israel had been thrown down and depressed, but he shall raise it out of the dust. <div eID="gen20855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20856" type="x-p"/> 4. That he shall have a throne, and be both priest and king upon his throne. A throne denotes both dignity and dominion, an exalted honour with an extensive power. (1.) This priest shall be a king, and his office as a priest shall be no diminution to his dignity as a king: <hi type="italic">He shall sit and rule upon his throne.</hi> Christ, as a priest, ever lives to make intercession for us; but he does it sitting at his Father's right hand, as one having authority, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.1">Heb. viii. 1</reference>. We have <hi type="italic">such a high priest</hi> as Israel never had, for he is <hi type="italic">set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens,</hi> which puts a prevailing virtue into his mediation; he that appears for us within the veil is one that sits and rules there. Christ, who is ordained to offer sacrifices for us, is authorized to give law to us. He will not save us unless we be willing that he should govern us. God has prepared him a throne <hi type="italic">in the heavens;</hi> and, if we would have any benefit by that, we must prepare him a throne in our hearts, and be willing and glad that he should <hi type="italic">sit and rule upon that throne;</hi> and to him every thought within us must be brought into obedience. (2.) This king shall be a priest, a <hi type="italic">priest upon his throne.</hi> With the majesty and power of a king, he shall have the tenderness and simplicity of a priest, who, being <hi type="italic">taken from among men,</hi> is <hi type="italic">ordained for men,</hi> and <hi type="italic">can have compassion on the ignorant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.5.1-Heb.5.2">Heb. v. 1, 2</reference>. In all the acts of his government as a king he prosecutes the intentions of his grace as a priest. Let not therefore those that are his look upon his throne, though a throne of glory and a throne of judgment, with terror and amazement; for, as there is a <hi type="italic">rainbow about the throne,</hi> so he is a <hi type="italic">priest upon the throne.</hi> <div eID="gen20856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20857" type="x-p"/> 5. That <hi type="italic">the counsel of peace shall be between them both.</hi> That is, (1.) Between <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> and the <hi type="italic">man the branch,</hi> between the Father and the Son; the counsels concerning the peace to be made between God and man, by the mediation of Christ, shall be concerted (that is, shall <hi type="italic">appear to have been</hi> concerted) by Infinite Wisdom in the covenant of redemption; the Father and the Son understood one another perfectly well in that matter. Or, rather, (2.) Between the priest and the throne, between the priestly and kingly office of Jesus Christ. <hi type="italic">The man the branch</hi> must grow up to carry on a <hi type="italic">counsel of peace,</hi> peace on earth, and, in order to that, peace with heaven. God's thoughts towards us were <hi type="italic">thoughts of peace,</hi> and, in prosecution of them, he exalted his Son Christ Jesus to be <hi type="italic">both a prince</hi> and a <hi type="italic">Saviour;</hi> he gave him a throne, but with this proviso, that he should be a priest upon his throne, and by executing the two offices of a priest and king should bring about that great undertaking of man's reconciliation to God and happiness in God. Some think it alludes to the former government of the Jews' state, wherein the king and priest, separate officers, did take counsel one with another, for the maintenance of peace and prosperity in church and state, as did Zerubbabel and Joshua now. I may add, the <hi type="italic">prophets of God helping them.</hi> So shall the peace and welfare of the gospel-church, and of all believers, be wrought, though not by two separate persons, yet by virtue of two separate offices meeting in one—Christ purchasing all peace by his priesthood and maintaining and defending it by his kingdom; so Mr. Pemble. And his prophetic office is serviceable to both in this great design. <div eID="gen20857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20858" type="x-p"/> 6. That there shall be a happy coalition between Jews and Gentiles in the gospel-church, and they shall both meet in Christ, the priest upon his throne, as the centre of their unity (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those that are far off shall come and build in the temple of the Lord.</hi> Some understand it of the Jews that were now afar off in Babylon, that staid behind in captivity, to the great discouragement of their brethren that had returned, who wanted their help in building the temple. Now God promises that many of them, and some of other nations too, proselyted to the Jewish religion, should come in, and lend a helping hand to the building of the temple, and many hands would make light work. The kings of Persia contributed to the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.8">Ezra vi. 8</reference>) and the furnishing of it, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.19-Ezra.7.20">Ezra vii. 19, 20</reference>. And, in after-times, Herod the Great, and others that were strangers, helped to beautify and enrich the temple. But it has a further reference to that <hi type="italic">temple of the Lord</hi> which <hi type="italic">the man the branch</hi> was to build. The Gentiles, <hi type="italic">strangers afar off,</hi> shall help to build it, for from among them God will raise up ministers that shall be workers together with Christ about that building; and all the Gentile converts shall be stones added to this building, so that it shall <hi type="italic">grow up to a holy temple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20-Eph.2.22">Eph. ii. 20-22</reference>. When God's temple is to be built he can fetch in those that are afar off and employ them in the building of it. <div eID="gen20858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20859" type="x-p"/> 7. That the accomplishment of this will be a strong confirmation of the truth of God's word: <hi type="italic">You shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me unto you.</hi> That promise, that those that were afar off should come and assist them in <hi type="italic">building the temple of the Lord,</hi> was as it were the <hi type="italic">giving of them a sign;</hi> by this they might be assured that the other promises should be fulfilled in due time. This should be fulfilled now very speedily; it was so, for those that had been their enemies and accusers, in obedience to the king's edict, became their helpers and did speedily what they were ordered to do for the furtherance of the work, and by that means the work went on and was finished; see <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.13-Ezra.6.14">Ezra vi. 13, 14</reference>. Now, by this surprising assistance which they had from afar off in building the temple, they might know that Zechariah, who told them of it before, was sent of God, and that therefore his word concerning the man the branch should be fulfilled. <div eID="gen20859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20860" type="x-p"/> 8. That these promises were strong obligations to obedience: "<hi type="italic">For this shall come to pass</hi> (you shall have help in building the temple) <hi type="italic">if you will diligently obey the voice of the Lord your God.</hi> You shall have the help of foreigners in building the temple, if you will but set about it in good earnest yourselves." The assistance of others, instead of being an excuse for our slothfulness, should be a spur to our industry. "You shall have the benefit and comfort of all those promises if you make conscience of your duty." They must know that they are upon their good behaviour; and, though their God is coming towards them in a way of mercy, they cannot expect him to proceed in it unless they conform to his laws. Note, That which God requires of us, to qualify us for his favour, is obedience to his revealed will; and it must be a diligent obedience. We cannot <hi type="italic">obey the voice of God</hi> without a great deal of care and pains, nor will our obedience be accepted of God unless it be laboured by us. <div eID="gen20860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20861" type="x-p"/> III. The provision that was made to preserve the remembrance of this. <hi type="italic">The crowns</hi> that were used in this solemnity were not given to Joshua, but must be <hi type="italic">kept for a memorial in the temple of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.6.14">v. 14</reference>. Either they were laid up in the temple treasury or (as the Jews' tradition is) they were hung up in the windows of the temple, in the view of all, <hi type="italic">in perpetuam rei memoriam—for a perpetual memorial,</hi> for a traditional evidence of the promise of the Messiah and this typical transaction used for the confirmation of that promise. The crowns were delivered to those who found the materials (and some think their names were engraven on the crowns), to be preserved as a public testimony of their pious liberality and an encouragement to others in like manner to bring presents to the house of God. Note, Various means were used for the support of the faith of the Old-Testament saints, who waited for the consolation of Israel, till the time, the set time, for it came.  <chapter eID="Zech.6"/> <div eID="gen20861" type="x-p"/>

entries.e0b352488aa6ebbc37b9ebc3c8bf346dc462fd43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13076"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.6.1-Zech.6.8">Zec 6:1-8</reference>. Eighth Vision. The Four Chariots.</title> <div sID="gen24571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13076"/><hi type="bold">1. four chariots--</hi>symbolizing the various dispensations of Providence towards the Gentile nations which had been more or less brought into contact with Judea; especially in punishing Babylon. Compare <reference osisRef="Zech.6.8">Zec 6:8</reference> ("the north country," that is, Babylon); <reference osisRef="Zech.1.15">Zec 1:15</reference>; 2:6. The number "four" is specified not merely in reference to the four quarters of the horizon (implying universal judgments), but in allusion to the four world kingdoms of Daniel.<div eID="gen24571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from between two mountains--</hi>the valley of Jehoshaphat, between Moriah and Mount Olivet [Moore]; or the valley between Zion and Moriah, where the Lord is (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.10">Zec 2:10</reference>), and whence He sends forth His ministers of judgment on the heathen [Maurer]. The temple on Mount Moriah is the symbol of the theocracy; hence the nearest spot accessible to chariots in the valley below is the most suitable for a vision affecting Judah in relation to the Gentile world powers. The chariot is the symbol of war, and so of judgments.<div eID="gen24572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24573" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of brass--</hi>the metal among the ancients representing hard solidity; so the immovable and resistless firmness of God's people (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.1.18">Jr 1:18</reference>). Calvin explains the "two mountains" thus: The secret purpose of God from eternity does not come forth to view before the execution, but is hidden and kept back irresistibly till the fit time, as it were between lofty mountains; the chariots are the various changes wrought in nations, which, as swift heralds, announce to us what before we knew not. The "two" may thus correspond to the number of the "olive trees" (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.3">Zec 4:3</reference>); the allusion to the "two mountains" near the temple is not necessarily excluded in this view. Henderson explains them to be the Medo-Persian kingdom, represented by the "two horns" (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.3">Da 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.4">4</reference>), now employed to execute God's purpose in punishing the nations; but the prophecy reaches far beyond those times. <div eID="gen24573" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc13828b89741f83e0390e83c00e33cae9ae8f9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13077"/><div sID="gen24574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13077"/><hi type="bold">2. red--</hi>implying carnage.<div eID="gen24574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">black--</hi>representing sorrow; also famine (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.5">Re 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.6">6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.1.8">Zec 1:8</reference>). <div eID="gen24575" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f39b20527c147049bf44bc100a550d439af714c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13078"/><div sID="gen24576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13078"/><hi type="bold">3. white--</hi>implying joy and victory [Calvin].<div eID="gen24576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grizzled--</hi>piebald. Implying a mixed dispensation, partly prosperity, partly adversity. All four dispensations, though various in character to the Gentile nation, portended alike good to God's people.<div eID="gen24577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bay--</hi>rather, "strong" or "fleet"; so Vulgate [Gesenius]. The horses have this epithet, whose part it was to "walk to and fro through the earth" (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.7">Zec 6:7</reference>). However, the Septuagint and Chaldee agree with English Version in referring the Hebrew to color, not strength. <div eID="gen24578" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc9108304bce93887495209da4d029255a57201b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13079"/><div sID="gen24579" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13079"/>4. The prophet humbly and teachably seeks instruction from God, and therefore seeks not in vain. <div eID="gen24579" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d8e4c9a748f29c1321cc2289ef2692e0cac8525: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13080"/><div sID="gen24580" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13080"/><hi type="bold">5. four spirits of the heavens--</hi>heavenly spirits who "stand before Jehovah" to receive God's commands (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.14">Zec 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.19">1Ki 22:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.1">Job 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.19">Lu 1:19</reference>) in heaven (of which Zion is the counterpart on earth, see on <reference osisRef="Zech.6.1">Zec 6:1</reference>), and proceed with chariot speed (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.17">2Ki 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference>) to execute them on earth in its four various quarters (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.4">Psa 104:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.7">He 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>) [Pembellus]. Or, the secret impulses of God which emanate from His counsel and providence; the prophet implies that all the revolutions in the world are from the Spirit of God and are as it were, His messengers or spirits [Calvin]. <div eID="gen24580" type="x-p"/>
entries.984fff3074a932f0a3f2105af00fdded3b481e96: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13081"/><div sID="gen24581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13081"/><hi type="bold">6. north country--</hi>Babylon (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.1.14">Jr 1:14</reference>). The north is the quarter specified in particular whence Judah and Israel are hereafter to return to their own land (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.6">Zec 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.18">Jr 3:18</reference>). "The black horses" go to Babylon, primarily to represent the awful desolation with which Darius visited it in the fifth year of his reign (two years after this prophecy) for revolting [Henderson]. The "white" go after the "black" horses to the same country; two sets being sent to it because of its greater cruelty and guilt in respect to Judea. The white represent Darius triumphant subjugation of it [Moore]. Rather, I think, the white are sent to victoriously subdue Medo-Persia, the second world kingdom, lying in the same quarter as Babylon, namely, north.<div eID="gen24581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grizzled ... toward the south--</hi>that is, to Egypt, the other great foe of God's people. It, being a part of the Græco-Macedonian kingdom, stands for the whole of it, the third world kingdom. <div eID="gen24582" type="x-p"/>
entries.85fe3507d086297d6f3a0f52084c5ff1275ed864: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13082"/><div sID="gen24583" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13082"/><hi type="bold">7. bay--</hi>rather, the "fleet" (or "strong"). As the "red" are not otherwise mentioned, the epithet "fleet" (as the Hebrew for "bay" ought to be translated) in <reference osisRef="Zech.6.3">Zec 6:3</reference> seems to apply to all four, and here especially to the "red." Their office is to complete hereafter the work already in part executed by the previous three who have stilled Babylon, Medo-Persia, and Græco-Macedonia; namely, to punish finally the last great foe of Israel, the final form assumed by the fourth world kingdom, Rome, which is to continue down to the second advent of Christ. Hence they "walk to and fro through the earth," counterworking Satan's "going to and fro in the earth" (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Ti 4:1</reference>), in connection with the last awful development of the fourth world kingdom. Their "fleetness" is needed to counteract his restless activity; their red color implies the final great carnage (<reference osisRef="Ezek.39.1-Ezek.39.29">Eze 39:1-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17">Re 19:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.21">18, 21</reference>). <div eID="gen24583" type="x-p"/>
entries.bcb52513a5456434954d7dd646c62b23b8372cce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13083"/><div sID="gen24584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13083"/><hi type="bold">8. north ... quieted ... my spirit--</hi>that is, caused My anger to rest (<reference osisRef="Judg.8.3">Jud 8:3</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.4">Ec 10:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.13">Eze 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.42">16:42</reference>). Babylon alone of the four great world kingdoms had in Zechariah's time been finally punished; therefore, in its case alone does God now say His anger is satisfied; the others had as yet to expiate their sin; the fourth has still to do so.<div eID="gen24584" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.6.9-Zech.6.15">Zec 6:9-15</reference>. Ninth Vision. The Crowning of Joshua.</title> <div sID="gen24585" type="x-p"/> The double crown is placed on Joshua's head, symbolizing that the true priesthood and the kingdom shall be conferred on the one Messiah. Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.6.20">He 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.7.1-Heb.7.21">7:1-21</reference>, on Melchisedek, who similarly combined the kingdom and priesthood as type of Messiah. <div eID="gen24585" type="x-p"/>
entries.739fca7ac34cbbbcf03e4e5cb3aa845fc2f94b26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13084"/><div sID="gen24586" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13084"/><hi type="bold">10. Take of them of the captivity--</hi>Take silver and gold (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.11">Zec 6:11</reference>) from them. The three named came from Babylon (where some of the exiled Jews still were left) to present gifts of silver and gold towards the building of the temple. But in <reference osisRef="Zech.6.11">Zec 6:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.14">14</reference>, "crowns" are directed to be made of them, then to be set on Joshua's head, and to be deposited in the temple as a memorial of the donors, until Messiah shall appear.<div eID="gen24586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Heldai--</hi>meaning "robust." Called Helem below.<div eID="gen24587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24588" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tobijah--</hi>that is, "the goodness of God."<div eID="gen24588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jedaiah--</hi>that is, "God knows."<div eID="gen24589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which are come from Babylon--</hi>This clause in the Hebrew comes after "Josiah son of Zephaniah." Therefore, Moore thinks Josiah as well as the three "came from Babylon." But as he has a "house" at Jerusalem, he is plainly a resident, not a visitor. Therefore English Version is right; or Maurer, "Josiah son of Zephaniah, to whom they are come (as guests) from Babylon."<div eID="gen24590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24591" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the same day--</hi>No time was to be lost to mark the significancy of their coming from afar to offer gifts to the temple, typifying, in the double crown made of their gifts and set on Joshua's head, the gathering in of Israel's outcasts to Messiah hereafter, who shall then be recognized as the true king and priest. <div eID="gen24591" type="x-p"/>
entries.258ba1899bd1dd79685c12b8fb8c2e651e1c1b31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13085"/><div sID="gen24592" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13085"/>11. The high priest wore a crown above the miter (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.5">Zec 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.8.9">Le 8:9</reference>). Messiah shall wear many crowns, one surmounting the other (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.12">Re 19:12</reference>). It was a thing before unknown in the Levitical priesthood that the same person should wear at once the crown of a king and that of a high priest (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.10">He 5:10</reference>). Messiah shall be revealed fully in this twofold dignity when He shall "restore the kingdom to Israel" (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.6">Ac 1:6</reference>). <div eID="gen24592" type="x-p"/>
entries.58bc3b7cc951a65da352ec03b38c88d3d9d4c54f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13086"/><div sID="gen24593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13086"/><hi type="bold">12. Behold, the man--</hi>namely, shall arise. Pilate unconsciously spake God's will concerning Him, "Behold the man" (<reference osisRef="John.19.5">Joh 19:5</reference>). The sense here is, "Behold in Joshua a remarkable shadowing forth of Messiah." It is not for his own sake that the crown is placed on him, but as type of Messiah about to be at once king and priest. Joshua could not individually be crowned king, not being of the royal line of David, but only in his representative character.<div eID="gen24593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Branch--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zec 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Is 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">33:15</reference>).<div eID="gen24594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall grow up out of his place--</hi>retaining the image of a "Branch"; "He shall sprout up from His place," that is, the place peculiar to Him: not merely from Beth-lehem or Nazareth, but by His own power, without man's aid, in His miraculous conception [Henderson]; a sense brought out in the original, "from under Himself," or "from (of) Himself" [Calvin]. Moore makes it refer to His growing lowly in His place of obscurity, "as a tender plant and a root out of a dry ground" (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Is 53:2</reference>), for thirty years unknown except as the son of a carpenter. Maurer translates, "Under Him there shall be growth (in the Church)." English Version accords better with the Hebrew (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.10.23">Ex 10:23</reference>). The idea in a Branch is that Christ's glory is growing, not yet fully manifested as a full-grown tree. Therefore men reject Him now.<div eID="gen24595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24596" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">build the temple--</hi>The promise of the future true building of the spiritual temple by Messiah (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.18">Mt 16:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.17">1Co 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2Co 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20-Eph.2.22">Ep 2:20-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.3.3">He 3:3</reference>) is an earnest to assure the Jews, that the material temple will be built by Joshua and Zerubbabel, in spite of all seeming obstacles. It also raises their thoughts beyond the material to the spiritual temple, and also to the future glorious temple, to be reared in Israel under Messiah's superintendence (Eze 40:1-43:27). The repetition of the same clause (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>) gives emphasis to the statement as to Messiah's work. <div eID="gen24596" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b85872615f5707cba61cee7563dafd99084b6d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13087"/><div sID="gen24597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13087"/><hi type="bold">13. bear the glory--</hi>that is, wear the insignia of the kingly glory, "the crowns" (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.5">Psa 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.16">102:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.13">Is 52:13</reference>). He himself shall bear the glory, not thou, Joshua, though thou dost bear the crowns. The Church's dignity is in her head alone, Christ. So Eliakim, type of Messiah, was to have "all the glory of his father's house hung upon him" (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.24">Is 22:24</reference>).<div eID="gen24597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sit--</hi>implying security and permanence.<div eID="gen24598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">priest ... throne--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.14.18">Ge 14:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.6">He 5:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.20">6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.7.1-Heb.7.28">7:1-28</reference>).<div eID="gen24599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24600" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">counsel of peace ... between ... both--</hi>Joshua and Zerubbabel, the religious and civil authorities co-operating in the temple, typify the peace, or harmonious union, between both the kingly and priestly offices. The kingly majesty shall not depress the priestly dignity, nor the priestly dignity the kingly majesty [Jerome]. The peace of the Church, formerly sought for in the mutual "counsels" of the kings and the priests, who had been always distinct, shall be perfectly ensured by the concurrence of the two offices in the one Messiah, who by His mediatorial priesthood purchases it, and by His kingly rule maintains it. Vitringa takes "His throne" to be Jehovah the Father's. Thus it will be, "there shall be ... peace between the Branch and Jehovah" [Ludovicus De Dieu]. The other view is better, namely, "Messiah's throne." As Priest He expiates sin; as King, extirpates it. "Counsel of peace," implies that it is the plan of infinite "wisdom," whence Messiah is called "Counsellor" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.8">Ep 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.17">He 6:17</reference>). Peace between the kingly and priestly attributes of Messiah implies the harmonizing of the conflicting claims of God's justice as a King, and His love as a Father and Priest. Hence is produced peace to man (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Lu 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.10.36">Ac 10:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.13-Eph.2.17">Ep 2:13-17</reference>). It is only by being pardoned through His atonement and ruled by His laws, that we can find "peace." The royal "throne" was always connected with the "temple," as is the case in the Apocalypse (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.15">Re 7:15</reference>), because Christ is to be a king on His throne and a priest, and because the people, whose "king" the Lord is, cannot approach Him except by a priestly mediation [Roos]. Jesus shall come to effect, by His presence (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.17">Da 7:17</reference>), that which in vain is looked for, in His absence, by other means. He shall exercise His power mediatorially as priest on His throne (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>); therefore His reign is for a limited period, which it could not be if it were the final and everlasting state of glory. But being for a special purpose, to reconcile all things in this world, now disordered by sin, and so present it to God the Father that He may again for the first time since the fall come into direct connection with His creatures; therefore it is limited, forming the dispensation in the fulness of times (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>), when God shall gather in one all things in Christ, the final end of which shall be, "God all in all" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24-1Cor.15.28">1Co 15:24-28</reference>). <div eID="gen24600" type="x-p"/>
entries.8421feae4a2752c0f4818c203e48774a7fbf804f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13088"/><div sID="gen24601" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13088"/><hi type="bold">14. the crowns shall be to Helem ... a memorial--</hi>deposited in the temple, to the honor of the donors; a memorial, too, of the coronation of Joshua, to remind all of Messiah, the promised antitypical king-priest, soon to come. Helem, the same as Heldai above. So Hen (that is, "favor") is another name for Josiah (that is, "God founds") above. The same person often had two names. <div eID="gen24601" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e08a1c8c64fbf631d8575d5a6476cfaa14f4699: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13089"/><div sID="gen24602" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13089"/><hi type="bold">15. they ... far off shall ... build--</hi>The reason why the crowns were made of gold received from afar, namely, from the Jews of Babylon, was to typify the conversion of the Gentiles to Messiah, King of Israel. This, too, was included in the "peace" spoken of in <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.39">Ac 2:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.12-Eph.2.17">Ep 2:12-17</reference>). Primarily, however, the return of the dispersed Israelites "from afar" (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.9">Is 60:9</reference>) to the king of the Jews at Jerusalem is intended, to be followed, secondly, by the conversion of the Gentiles from "far off" (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.11">Zec 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.2-2Cor.8.2">8:2-2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.10">Is 60:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">57:19</reference>).<div eID="gen24602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24603" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">build in the temple--</hi>Christ "builds the temple" (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.12">Zec 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.3.3">He 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.4">4</reference>): His people "build in the temple." Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.3.2">He 3:2</reference>, "Moses in His house."<div eID="gen24603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye shall know, &c.--</hi>when the event corresponds to the prediction (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.9">Zec 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.9">4:9</reference>).<div eID="gen24604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this shall come to pass, if ye ... obey, &c.--</hi>To the Jews of Zechariah's day a stimulus is given to diligent prosecution of the temple building, the work which it was meanwhile their duty to fulfil, relying on the hope of the Messiah afterwards to glorify it. The completion of the temple shall "come to pass," if ye diligently on your part "obey the Lord." It is not meant that their unbelief could set aside God's gracious purpose as to Messiah's coming. But there is, secondarily, meant, that Messiah's glory as priest-king of Israel shall not be manifested to the Jews till they turn to Him with obedient penitence. They meanwhile are cast away "branches" until they be grafted in again on the Branch and their own olive tree (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zec 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10-Zech.12.12">12:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.39">Mt 23:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.16-Rom.11.24">Ro 11:16-24</reference>). <chapter eID="Zech.6"/>

entries.f2e3f35c0e0ecc15e05c173c9386d88a0e311fec: <div eID="gen35516" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35517" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35518" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35518" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35517" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35519" type="x-p"/> The vision of the four chariots drawn by several sorts of horses, <reference osisRef="Zac.6.1-Zac.6.8">Zac 6:1-8</reference>. The other vision in thus chapter may refer in its primary sense to the establishment of the civil and religious polity of the Jews under Joshua and Zerubbabel; but relates in a fuller sense, to the Messiah, and to that spiritual kingdom of which he was to be both king and high priest. In him all these types and figures were verified; on him all the promises are yea and amen, <reference osisRef="Zac.6.9-Zac.6.15">Zac 6:9-15</reference>. <div eID="gen35519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35520" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35521" type="x-p"/> There came four chariots - Four monarchies or empires. This is supposed to mean the same with the vision of the four horns, in chap. 1. <div eID="gen35521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35522" type="x-p"/> Mountains of brass - The strong barriers of God's purposes, which restrained those powers within the times and limits appointed by Jehovah.
entries.e28955e5e6e1028d5cd0bcfe992ce9296ae02a69: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35523" type="x-p"/> In the first chariot were red horses - The empire of the Chaldeans, which overthrew the empire of the Assyrians. <div eID="gen35523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35524" type="x-p"/> The second chariot black horses - The empire of the Persians founded by Cyrus, which destroyed the empire of the Chaldeans.
entries.b7c1c7871cb33b78c56a9ebd56d0de58ea3d6953: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen35524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35525" type="x-p"/> The third chariot white horses - The empire of the Greeks, founded by Alexander the Great, which destroyed the empire of the Persians. <div eID="gen35525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35526" type="x-p"/> The fourth chariot grisled and bay horses - That is party-coloured horses, or with horses, some grisled and some bay. The empire of the Romans or of the Greeks. The Greeks divided after the death of Alexander; one part pointing out the Lagidae, who attacked and subdued Egypt; and the other, the seleucidae, who subdued Syria under Seleucus.
entries.9a8f56d080f0e709d224d121e2f5bc7f75178711: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35527" type="x-p"/> The four spirits of the heavens - Ministers of God's wrath against the sinful nations of the world.
entries.10ec2289915efac070f0f3cd4113ee6f4cdaae6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35528" type="x-p"/> The black horses - This refers to the second chariot; of the first the angel makes no mention, because the empire designed by it had ceased to exist. This had red horses, to show the cruelty of the Chaldeans towards the Jews, and the carnage they committed in the land of Judea. <div eID="gen35528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35529" type="x-p"/> The black - Cyrus, at the head of the Persians and Medes, bringing devastation and death among the Chaldeans, called the north in many parts of Scripture. <div eID="gen35529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35530" type="x-p"/> The white - Alexander, who was splendid in his victories, and mild towards all that he conquered. <div eID="gen35530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35531" type="x-p"/> The grisled - The Lagidae or Ptolemies, who founded an empire in Egypt; of these some were good, some bad, some despotic, some moderate, some cruel, and some mild, represented by the party-coloured horses.
entries.7041986845cc42c308c42670c42c367c42f70fec: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35532" type="x-p"/> And the bay went forth - The Seleucidae, who conquered Syria and the upper provinces, and who wished to extend their conquests, and "sought to go, that they might walk to and fro throughout the earth," were of unbounded ambition, and sought universal empire; such as Antiochus the Great. "So they walked to and fro," did extend their conquests; and harassed many countries by their vexatious and almost continual wars. Some think the Romans are meant, who carried their conquests hither and thither, just as the Divine providence permitted them.
entries.ec6b8d9b26759f33acc27476b48dbbb11edc2c38: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35533" type="x-p"/> Have quieted my spirit in the north country - They have fulfilled my judgments on Assyria and Chaldea. Nabopolassar and Cyrus first, against the Assyrians and Chaldeans; and Alexander next, against the Persians. On this vision Abp. Newcome remarks: - <div eID="gen35533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35534" type="x-p"/> The black horses seem to denote the Persian empire; which, by subduing the Chaldeans, and being about to inflict a second heavy chastisement on Babylon, quieted God's spirit with respect to Chaldea; a country always spoken of as lying to the north of the Jews. <div eID="gen35534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35535" type="x-p"/> The white horses seem to be the Macedonian empire; which, like the Persian, overcame Chaldea. <div eID="gen35535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35536" type="x-p"/> The spotted bay horses seem to be the Roman empire. This description suits it because it was governed by kings, consuls, dictators, and emperors. It penetrated southward to Egypt and Africa. The Roman empire is mentioned twice, <reference osisRef="Zac.6.6">Zac 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zac.6.7">Zac 6:7</reference>, under each epithet given it, <reference osisRef="Zac.6.3">Zac 6:3</reference>.
entries.6dbba3cb477715aa9a46d180bee3d471af696cb5: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35537" type="x-p"/> Take of them of the captivity - The names that follow were probably those to whom the silver and golden vessels of the temple were intrusted; and who might have had bullion of silver and gold, for particular purposes, about the ornaments of the temple. <div eID="gen35537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35538" type="x-p"/> The house of Josiah - Probably an artificer in silver, gold, etc.
entries.d0081bfb5540f7586c4a1d0ad5372306f17d0797: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen35538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35539" type="x-p"/> Make crowns - עטרות ataroth; but seven MSS. of Kennicott's and De Rossi's, and one ancient of my own, with the Syriac and Chaldee, have עטרת atereth, a crown, or tiara. And as Joshua the high priest is alone concerned here, I think one crown only is intended.
entries.c386698be038480380d73a683ab0ea6ecd682dbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35540" type="x-p"/> Behold the man whose name is The Branch! - I cannot think that Zerubbabel is here intended; indeed, he is not so much as mentioned in <reference osisRef="Zac.3.8">Zac 3:8</reference>. Joshua and his companions are called אנשי מופת anshey mopheth, figurative or typical men; the crowning therefore of Joshua in this place, and calling him the Branch, was most probably in reference to that glorious person, the Messiah, of whom he was the type or figure. The Chaldee has, "whose name is my Messiah," or Christ. <div eID="gen35540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35541" type="x-p"/> And he shall grow up out of his place - That is, out of David's root, tribe, and family. <div eID="gen35541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35542" type="x-p"/> And he shall build the temple of the Lord - This cannot refer to the building of the temple then in hand, for Zerubbabel was its builder: but to that temple, the Christian Church, that was typified by it; for Zerubbabel is not named here, and only Joshua or Jesus (the name is the same) is the person who is to be crowned and to build this spiritual temple.
entries.f55dde609e878116b833c8fd2327ad482f9f7325: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen35542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35543" type="x-p"/> Even he shall build the temple - Joshua, not Zerubbabel. <div eID="gen35543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35544" type="x-p"/> He shall bear the glory - Have all the honor of it; for none can do this but himself. The Messiah is still intended. <div eID="gen35544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35545" type="x-p"/> And shall sit and rule upon his throne - For the government of the Church shall be upon his shoulder. <div eID="gen35545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35546" type="x-p"/> And he shall be a priest upon his throne - He shall, as the great high priest, offer the only available offering and atonement; and so he shall be both king and priest, a royal king and a royal priest; for even the priest is here stated to sit upon his throne. <div eID="gen35546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35547" type="x-p"/> And the counsel of peace shall be between them both - Whom? Zerubbabel and Joshua? Certainly not Zerubbabel, for he is not mentioned in all this prediction; but, as the Messiah is intended, the counsel of peace - the purpose to establish peace between heaven and earth, must be between the Father and the Son.
entries.7d7d7f71d70e2a9a54a45d25f761c89f54b98eee: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen35547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35548" type="x-p"/> And the crowns shall be - One of my MSS. has אטרות ataroth, crowns, corrected into עטרת atereth, crown; and so the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic. The Chaldee has, "And praise shall be," etc. The meaning appears to be this, that the crown made for Joshua should be delivered to the persons mentioned here and in <reference osisRef="Zac.6.10">Zac 6:10</reference>, to be laid up in the temple of the Lord, as a memorial of this typical transaction.
entries.d6a87e85b859ab31e00ac038a0d26b3395aa72ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen35548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35549" type="x-p"/> And they that are far off shall come - The Gentiles shall come to the Savior of the world; and build - become a part of this new temple; for they, as living stones, shall become a holy temple, a habitation of God through the Spirit. <div eID="gen35549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35550" type="x-p"/> Ye shall know that the Lord of hosts hath sent me - These predictions, relative to the regal and sacerdotal offices of the Messiah, shall be so circumstantially fulfilled, that ye, Jews, shall be obliged to acknowledge that the Lord of hosts hath sent me with this message. <div eID="gen35550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35551" type="x-p"/> And this shall come to pass - Your own temple shall be rebuilt, and God shall dwell among you now, if ye will diligently obey the voice of Jehovah your God.  <chapter eID="Zech.6"/> <div eID="gen35551" type="x-p"/>

entries.724ab22f8874865925b8fca722913a8197835ec7: Zec 6:1-8 <div eID="gen16831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16832" type="x-p"/> Zec 6:1. <hi type="italic">“And again I lifted up my eyes, and saw, and behold four chariots coming forth between the two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of brass.</hi> Zec 6:2. <hi type="italic">In the first chariot were red horses, and in the second chariot black horses.</hi> Zec 6:3. <hi type="italic">And in the third chariot white horses, and in the fourth chariot speckled powerful horses.</hi> Zec 6:4. <hi type="italic">And I answered and said to the angel that talked with me, What are these, my lord?</hi> Zec 6:5. <hi type="italic">And the angel answered and said to me, These are the four winds of heaven going out, after having stationed themselves by the Lord of the whole earth.</hi> Zec 6:6. <hi type="italic">Those in which the black horses are, go out into the land of the north, and the white have gone out behind them, and the speckled have gone out into the land of the south.</hi> Zec 6:7. <hi type="italic">And the powerful ones have gone out, and sought to go, to pass through the earth; and he said, Go ye, and pass through the earth; and they passed through the earth.</hi> Zec 6:8. <hi type="italic">And he called to me, and spake to me thus: Behold, those which go out into the land of the north let down my spirit in the land of the north.” </hi> The four chariots are explained in Zec 6:5 by the interpreting angel to be the four winds of heaven, which go forth after they have taken their stand by the Lord of the whole earth, i.e., have appeared before Him in the attitude of servants, to lay their account before Him, and to receive commands from Him (התיצּב על, as in <reference osisRef="Job.1.6">Job 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.1">Job 2:1</reference>). This addition shows that the explanation is not a real interpretation; that is to say, the meaning is not that the chariots represent the four winds; but the less obvious figure of the chariots is explained through the more obvious figure of the winds, which answers better to the reality. Since, for example, according to Zec 6:8, the chariots are designed to carry the Spirit (<hi type="italic">rūăch</hi>) of God, there was nothing with which they could be more suitably compared than the winds (<hi type="italic">rūăch</hi>) of heaven, for these are the most appropriate earthly substratum to symbolize the working of the Divine Spirit (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.49.36">Jer 49:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.2">Dan 7:2</reference>). This Spirit, in its judicial operations, is to be borne by the chariots to the places more immediately designated in the vision. As they go out, after having appeared before God, the two mountains, between which they go out or come forth, can only be sought in the place where God’s dwelling is. But the mountains are of brass, and therefore are not earthly mountains; but they are not therefore mere symbols of the might of God with which His church is defended (Hengst., Neumann), or allusions to the fact that the dwelling-place of God is immovable and unapproachable (Koehler), or symbols of the imperial power of the world and the kingdom of God (Kliefoth), according to which the power of the world would be just as immovable as the kingdom of God. The symbol has rather a definite geographical view as its basis. As the lands to which the chariots go are described geographically as the lands of the north and south, the starting-point of the chariots must also be thought of geographically, and must therefore be a place or country lying between the northern and southern lands: this is the land of Israel, or more especially Jerusalem, the centre of the Old Testament kingdom of God, where the Lord had His dwelling-place. It is therefore the view of Jerusalem and its situation that lies at the foundation of the vision; only we must not think of the mountains Zion and Moriah (as Osiander, Maurer, Hofmann, and Umbreit do), for these are never distinguished from one another in the Old Testament as forming two separate mountains; but we have rather to think of Zion and the Mount of Olives, which stood opposite to it towards the east. Both are named as places where or from which the Lord judges the world, viz., the Mount of Olives in Zec 14:4, and Zion very frequently, e.g., in Joe 3:16. The place between the two mountains is, then, the valley of Jehoshaphat, in which, according to Joe 3:2., the Lord judges the nations. In the vision before us this valley simply forms the starting-point for the chariots, which carry the judgment from the dwelling-place of God into the lands of the north and south, which are mentioned as the seat of the imperial power; and the mountains are of brass, to denote the immovable firmness of the place where the Lord dwells, and where He has founded His kingdom. <div eID="gen16832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16833" type="x-p"/> The colour of the horses, by which the four chariots are distinguished, is just as significant here as in Zec 1:8; and indeed, so far as the colour is the same, the meaning is also the same here as there. Three colours are alike, since <hi type="italic">beruddı̄m</hi>, speckled, is not essentially different from <hi type="italic">seruqqı̄m</hi>, starling-grey, viz., black and white mixed together (see at Zec 1:8). The black horses are added here. Black is the colour of grief (cf. “black as sackcloth of hair,” <reference osisRef="Rev.6.12">Rev 6:12</reference>). The rider upon the black horse in <reference osisRef="Rev.6.5-Rev.6.6">Rev 6:5-6</reference>, holds in his hand the emblem of dearness, the milder form of famine. Consequently the colours of the horses indicate the destination of the chariots, to execute judgment upon the enemies of the kingdom of God. Red, as the colour of blood, points to war and bloodshed; the speckled colour to pestilence and other fatal plagues; and the black colour to dearness and famine: so that these three chariots symbolize the three great judgments, war, pestilence, and hunger (2Sa 24:11.), along with which “the noisome beast” is also mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.21">Eze 14:21</reference> as a fourth judgment. In the vision before us the fourth chariot is drawn by white horses, to point to the glorious victories of the ministers of the divine judgment. The explanation of the chariots in this vision is rendered more difficult by the fact, that on the one hand the horses of the fourth chariot are not only called <hi type="italic">beruddı̄m</hi>, but אמצּים also; and on the other hand, that in the account of the starting of the chariots the red horses are omitted, and the speckled are distinguished from the אמשצים instead, inasmuch as it is affirmed of the former that they went forth into the south country, and of the latter, that “they sought to go that they might pass through the whole earth,” and they passed through with the consent of God. The commentators have therefore attempted in different ways to identify האמשצים in Zec 6:7 with אדמּים. Hitzig and Maurer assume that אמצים is omitted from Zec 6:6 by mistake, and that אמצים in Zec 6:7 is a copyist’s error for אדמים, although there is not a single critical authority that can be adduced in support of this. Hengstenberg and Umbreit suppose that the predicate אמצּים, strong, in Zec 6:3 refers to all the horses in the four chariots, and that by the “strong” horses of Zec 6:7 we are to understand the “red” horses of the first chariot. But if the horses of all the chariots were strong, the red alone cannot be so called, since the article not only stands before אמצּים in Zec 6:7, but also before the three other colours, and indicates nothing more than that the colours have been mentioned before. Moreover, it is grammatically impossible that אמצּים in Zec 6:3 should refer to all the four teams; as “we must in that case have had אמצּים כּלּם” (Koehler). Others (e.g., Abulw., Kimchi, Calvin, and Koehler) have attempted to prove that אמצּים taht evo may have the sense of אדמּים; regarding אמוּץ as a softened form of חמוּץ, and explaining the latter, after <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Isa 63:1</reference>, as signifying bright red. But apart from the fact that it is impossible to see why so unusual a word should have been chosen in the place of the intelligible word <hi type="italic">'ădummı̄m</hi> in the account of the destination of the red team in Zec 6:7, unless אמשצים were merely a copyist’s error for <hi type="italic">'ădummı̄m</hi>, there are no satisfactory grounds for identifying אמץ with חמוּץ, since it is impossible to adduce any well-established examples of the change of ח into א in Hebrew. The assertion of Koehler, that the Chaldee verb אלם, <hi type="italic">robustus fuit</hi>, is חלם in Hebrew in <reference osisRef="Job.39.4">Job 39:4</reference>, is incorrect; for we find חלם in the sense of to be healthy and strong in the Syriac and Talmudic as well, and the Chaldaic אלם is a softened form of עלם, and not of חלם. The fact that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.35">1Ch 8:35</reference> we have the name תּארע in the place of תּחרע in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.41">1Ch 9:41</reference>, being the only instance of the interchange of א and ח in Hebrew, is not sufficient of itself to sustain the alteration, amidst the great mass of various readings in the genealogies of the Chronicles.
